title: Light, mirrors, lenses and refraction
blurb: Order the electromagnetic spectrum, apply the law of reflection, describe plane, concave and convex mirror images, and explain refraction, total internal reflection and corrective lenses.
question: Why are X-rays ionizing when radio waves are not, why does a store's security mirror show a small, wide view, and which lens helps a student who can read her notes but cannot see the board?

teach.body: Formally, light is a transverse electromagnetic wave. In a vacuum every electromagnetic wave travels at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s; in matter light slows down. Light also behaves as particles called photons, and a photon's energy rises with its frequency. In plain English: all of these waves are the same kind of thing at the same speed in space; they differ in wavelength and frequency, and the high-frequency ones pack the most energy.

teach.h: The electromagnetic spectrum (low to high frequency)
teach.caption: Left to right: frequency and photon energy rise, wavelength shrinks. All travel at c in a vacuum.

teach.body: Visible light runs red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (ROYGBIV). Red has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency; violet the shortest wavelength and highest frequency. White light is a mix of all of them. A prism separates the colors by dispersion, because each color refracts by a slightly different amount. An object's color is the light it reflects: a green leaf reflects green and absorbs the rest.

Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface), not from the surface. A ray at 30° to the normal leaves at 30° to the normal. A plane (flat) mirror forms a virtual, upright, same-size image, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, reversed left to right. Stand 2 m from a mirror and your image is 2 m behind it, 4 m from you.

rows.label: Image
values: Real, inverted; or magnified upright up close

teach.body: Refraction is the bending of light when it changes speed entering a new medium. The index of refraction n = c ÷ v (vacuum 1; water about 1.33; glass about 1.5: the stem gives values). Entering a slower medium (higher n), light bends toward the normal; entering a faster one, it bends away. Frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength change. With n = 1.5, v = 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 1.5 = 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Beyond the critical angle, light inside the denser medium is totally reflected: total internal reflection in fiber optics and endoscopes.

head: Lens
Shape and effect
Uses
teach.caption: The eye's cornea and lens form a real, inverted image on the retina; the brain reads it upright. Nearsighted (myopia): clear near, blurry far, concave lens. Farsighted (hyperopia): clear far, blurry near, convex lens.

teach.body: Jasmine, a radiography applicant, notes that X-rays sit far above visible light in frequency, so each photon carries enough energy to ionize atoms, while radio waves do not. Between classes she can read her notes but not the whiteboard: she is nearsighted, and concave (diverging) lenses spread the light so distant images focus on her retina. The clinic's endoscope carries light through flexible fibers by total internal reflection.

teach.text: Spectrum order: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma (do not swap X-ray and gamma or visible and infrared). Red has a LOWER frequency than violet. All EM waves travel at c in a vacuum. Measure angles from the normal. Plane-mirror images are virtual and upright. Convex mirrors shrink; concave mirrors can magnify. Convex lenses fix farsightedness; concave lenses fix nearsightedness. Refraction keeps the frequency.

items: EM spectrum by rising frequency and energy: radio, microwave, IR, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma; all at c in a vacuum.
Visible: red longest wavelength and lowest frequency; violet shortest and highest.
Angle of incidence = angle of reflection, from the normal; plane-mirror image virtual, upright, same size.
Concave mirror converges (can magnify); convex mirror diverges (smaller, wide view).
Slower medium: bends toward the normal, n = c/v. Convex lens fixes farsightedness; concave fixes nearsightedness.

summary: You can now order the electromagnetic spectrum by frequency, wavelength and photon energy and compare the colors of visible light. You can also apply the law of reflection, describe the images from plane, concave and convex mirrors, predict how light bends on refraction and choose the lens that corrects nearsightedness or farsightedness.

A.q: Which color of visible light has the highest frequency?
A.why: Violet has the shortest wavelength and the highest frequency of visible light.

whyNot.0: Red has the lowest frequency (longest wavelength).
whyNot.1: Yellow is in the middle of the spectrum, below violet.
whyNot.2: Green is in the middle of the spectrum, below violet.

A.q: A light ray strikes a plane mirror at 40° from the normal. What is the angle of reflection, measured from the normal?
A.why: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both from the normal: 40°.

whyNot.0: 50° is the angle measured from the mirror's surface, not from the normal.
whyNot.2: 80° is the angle between the incoming and reflected rays, not the angle of reflection.
whyNot.3: Halves the angle; reflection keeps it the same.

A.why: A farsighted eye focuses near objects behind the retina. A convex (converging) lens adds focusing power and corrects it.

whyNot.2: A flat plate does not change the eye's focus.
whyNot.3: A prism bends and disperses light; it does not correct focus.

B.q: Light passes from water into air. How does its path change?
options: It slows and bends toward the normal
It speeds up and bends toward the normal
It speeds up and bends away from the normal
It slows and bends away from the normal
B.why: Air has a lower index of refraction than water, so light speeds up and bends away from the normal.

whyNot.0: Light slows when entering water, not when leaving it for air.
whyNot.1: Speeding up bends light away from the normal, not toward it.
whyNot.3: Light speeds up in air, so it does not slow.

B.q: Which kind of mirror is used as a car's passenger-side mirror to give a wide field of view?
B.why: A convex mirror diverges light, giving a smaller, upright, virtual image of a wide area.

whyNot.0: A plane mirror gives a same-size image with a narrower field of view.
whyNot.2: A concave mirror converges light and can magnify; it narrows the view.
whyNot.3: Two plane mirrors still give same-size images, not a wide reduced view.

B.q: Why does a straw look bent where it enters a glass of water?
options: Light reflects off the water's surface
Water absorbs some colors of light
Light refracts as its speed changes
B.why: Light from the underwater part of the straw changes speed at the water surface and bends (refracts), so the straw appears broken.

whyNot.0: Reflection from the surface would show the straw's mirror image, not a bend.
whyNot.1: Absorption changes color or brightness, not the apparent position.
whyNot.2: Diffraction is spreading around edges; it does not shift the straw's image.

C.q: Light travels through a liquid at 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s. Using c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, what is the liquid's index of refraction? (n = c/v)

whyNot.0: Inverts the formula (v ÷ c); n is at least 1 for any material.
whyNot.2: Adds the two speeds' coefficients instead of dividing.

C.q: A patient stands 3.0 m in front of a plane mirror, then walks 1.0 m toward it. How far is she now from her image?
C.why: She is now 2.0 m from the mirror, and her image is 2.0 m behind it: 2.0 + 2.0 = 4.0 m.

whyNot.0: 2.0 m is her distance to the mirror, not to her image.
whyNot.1: 6.0 m was the distance before she moved.
whyNot.3: Subtracts her 1.0 m step once; the image also moves 1.0 m closer.

C.q: Which list orders these from lowest to highest photon energy?
C.why: Photon energy rises with frequency: infrared < visible < ultraviolet < X-ray.

whyNot.1: This runs from highest to lowest energy.
whyNot.2: Infrared has a lower frequency, and less energy, than visible light.
whyNot.3: X-rays have a higher frequency, and more energy, than ultraviolet.

reteach.title: The marching band hits the mud
reteach.question: A marching band crosses at an angle from pavement onto a muddy field. Why does the line of marchers swing to a new direction?

blocks.body: The marchers who reach the mud first slow down while those still on pavement keep their pace, so the line pivots and heads in a new direction, turned toward the normal. Light does the same at the edge of glass or water: the part of the wave that enters the slower medium first lags, so the beam bends toward the normal. Coming back out onto pavement (a faster medium), the line swings away from the normal again. The drumbeat (frequency) never changes.

blocks.text: Slower medium: toward the normal. Faster medium: away from the normal. The frequency stays the same; the wavelength shrinks in the slower medium.

explain.body: Radio waves have the longest wavelength; gamma rays the shortest. Frequency runs the opposite way.

test.q: Which of these electromagnetic waves has the longest wavelength?
test.why: Radio waves sit at the low-frequency, long-wavelength end of the spectrum.

whyNot.0: Microwaves are long, but radio waves are longer still.
whyNot.2: Visible light is in the middle of the spectrum.
whyNot.3: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength.

explain.body: Virtual, upright, same size, as far behind the mirror as you are in front, reversed left to right.

test.q: What kind of image does a flat bathroom mirror form?
test.why: A plane mirror forms a virtual, upright image the same size as the object.

whyNot.0: Plane mirrors do not form real, inverted images.
whyNot.1: A smaller virtual image comes from a convex mirror.
whyNot.3: Plane mirrors neither magnify nor form real images.

explain.body: Crossing into a new medium changes light's speed, wavelength and (at an angle) direction. Its frequency is set by the source and stays the same.

test.q: When light passes from air into water, which quantity stays the same?
test.why: Frequency is set by the source and does not change on refraction; speed and wavelength both decrease in water.

whyNot.1: The wavelength shortens as the speed falls.
whyNot.2: At an angle, the ray bends toward the normal.

explain.h: Matching the lens to the eye
explain.body: Blurry far (nearsighted): concave lens. Blurry near (farsighted): convex lens.

test.q: A man reads distant road signs easily but holds a menu at arm's length to read it. What is his condition, and which lens corrects it?
test.why: Clear far vision with blurry near vision is farsightedness (hyperopia), corrected by a convex (converging) lens.

whyNot.1: Nearsighted people see near objects clearly; he sees far objects clearly.
whyNot.2: Farsighted is right, but a concave lens would make near focus worse.
whyNot.3: He is not nearsighted, and a convex lens does not correct nearsightedness.
